title: Pricing by hours per project for Furniture restoration
audience: Owners and supervisors who write quotes for cleaning projects and need a price that covers cost and earns a margin.
learningOutcomes: Calculate a cost per productive hour from the owner's own figures
Estimate project hours, including set-up, travel and checking time
Build a quote from hours, a rate and a margin, and state its basis and exclusions

instruction.heading: Why hours are the starting unit
instruction.body: Furniture restoration time depends on the piece: the joints to re-glue, the veneer to lift, the finish to strip, and the hardware to clean and refit. The same chair can take a short or a long visit depending on damage. Hours make that visible, so the cost, the margin and the effect of a change in damage are clear. No source read for this course gives furniture restoration hours. The Airtasker item ranges are advertised prices by item type, not time, so the hours on each piece must come from your own records.

instruction.heading: Build the cost per productive hour
instruction.body: Take the total cost of running the business over a period and divide it by the productive hours in the same period. Include wages with on-costs such as leave and superannuation where your arrangements need them (business.gov.au, 1 October 2026), vehicle running costs, workshop and storage, abrasives, strippers, finishes, glue, upholstery materials as consumables, insurance, administration and premises. Productive hours are chargeable hours on a piece, not the paid hours on a roster. If you pay for 40 hours and 30 are chargeable, the cost per productive hour is higher than the hourly wage.

instruction.heading: Estimate the hours
instruction.body: Break each piece into stages: inspection, collection, disassembly, joint repair, stripping, sanding, finishing coats, hardware, and return delivery. Estimate each stage at a standard speed, then add set-up, pack-down, travel and a checking allowance. Xero's guide suggests adding 10 to 20 percent to job estimates for unexpected work (Xero Australia, 3 September 2026). That is a range to test against your own records, not a figure sourced for furniture. Record the actual hours for each piece and the reason for any difference, and correct the next estimate.

instruction.heading: Turn hours into a price
instruction.body: Multiply the crew hours by the cost per productive hour to get the cost of the job. Add a margin that reflects your target and the risk in the job, such as hidden damage, old finishes that need extra work, or a difficult collection. Apply your materials policy and your minimum charge. Then check the result against the sourced item ranges as a sense check. The Airtasker guide gives a dining table at $500 to $1,100 and a dining chair at $50 to $100 (Airtasker, 17 April 2025). A price well outside the range for that item needs a reason you can state.

instruction.heading: Keep the quote honest
instruction.body: A quote states the scope, the hours or price basis, the exclusions, what the client must provide, and how long the quote is valid. Exclusions for furniture work usually include hidden damage found after inspection, which is priced as a change, and any lead-related testing or safe-work method for old painted pieces. Do not show the internal cost per hour to the client unless your policy says to. Re-quote when the scope changes.

instruction.heading: Review your estimates
instruction.body: Compare estimated and actual hours for at least the first ten pieces of each type. If the variance is consistently above your agreed threshold, change the standard time, the margin or the scope rules. A pricing method is finished only when actual hours match quoted hours closely enough for the work to make money.

procedure: Gather the year's total business costs and the chargeable hours achieved in the same period.
Divide total costs by chargeable hours to get the cost per productive hour.
Break each piece into stages and estimate each stage time as a range.
Add set-up, pack-down, travel and checking time as named lines.
Multiply total crew hours by the cost per productive hour, then apply the margin for risk and target.
Apply the materials policy, the exclusions for hidden damage and the minimum charge.
Write the quote with scope, hours basis, exclusions, client inputs and validity.
Record actual hours after each job and compare them with the estimate.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative figures only, not market rates. A family brings in a dining table and four chairs. The estimate is 10 crew-hours for the table and 3 hours for each chair, 22 crew-hours in total, including inspection, set-up and checking. The cost per productive hour is $60 AUD (illustrative). The target margin on price is 25 per cent (illustrative).
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the cost of the job, what is the price with a 25 per cent margin on price, and does that price sit where the sourced item ranges say it should?
workedExamples.reasoning: The cost is 22 crew-hours multiplied by $60 AUD, which is $1,320 AUD. A 25 per cent margin on price means the price is the cost divided by 0.75, which gives $1,760 AUD. The Airtasker item ranges put the table at $500 to $1,100 and four chairs at $50 to $100 each, which is $700 to $1,500 together (Airtasker, 17 April 2025). The illustrative price is above that combined range. The owner checks whether the damage is heavier than the sourced range assumes, whether the 22 hours are right, and whether the chairs need a different stage plan. The gap is the lesson, not a price to publish.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative: an inspection-only visit to a damaged cabinet takes 1.5 crew-hours, including travel. The owner charges the inspection as a separate line and credits it against the job if the client accepts the quote.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the inspection's cost, and how should it appear on the quote?
workedExamples.reasoning: At the illustrative $60 AUD an hour, the 1.5 hours cost $90 AUD. At a 25 per cent margin on price, the inspection line would be $120 AUD. The owner shows it as a named line, states whether it is credited, and records the time, because the research did not source an inspection fee.

equipmentAndPpe: Quote worksheet or spreadsheet with stage hours for each piece
Time log for each piece, with estimated and actual columns
PPE as listed in {{business:safety.required_ppe}}, with the safety data sheet for each stripper and finish

commonErrors.error: Pricing from the hourly wage alone.
commonErrors.prevention: Include on-costs, workshop, strippers, finishes, glue, insurance and administration in the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Counting paid hours as productive hours.
commonErrors.prevention: Use chargeable hours only when calculating the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Leaving out collection, delivery, inspection and checking time. Gap: no sourced furniture hour standard exists.
commonErrors.prevention: Add these as named lines on every estimate.

commonErrors.error: Quoting with no exclusions for hidden damage or for lead-related work on old finishes.
commonErrors.prevention: List what is excluded, what is priced as a change, and what the client provides.

commonErrors.error: Never comparing estimates with actual hours.
commonErrors.prevention: Record actual hours after each job and review the variance monthly.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This is pricing guidance only. The ACCC says misleading statements about prices are prohibited under the Australian Consumer Law (ACCC, 15 July 2026). State or territory fair trading rules also apply and differ, so check the rules for your state.

NSW only: NSW LeadSmart says old painted furniture may carry lead, recommends a professional trained in lead paint work, and says wet sanding and wet scraping are the safest methods. Price any lead-related testing or safe-work method on its own line, and check the rule for the state where you work.

Victoria only: WorkSafe Victoria guidance (reviewed 17 April 2026) says wood dust is classed as carcinogenic to humans, that sanding needs local exhaust ventilation, and that a half-face P2 respirator would be sufficient in usual cases. Include dust controls and any respirator in the cost, and check the rule for your state.

Pay rates, allowances and on-costs for employees may be set by an award or enterprise agreement. Check which one applies to each worker before using any cost figure. This lesson does not state those rates.

qualityStandard: Each quote shows scope, hours or price basis, exclusions, client inputs and validity.
The cost per productive hour is calculated from the owner's own records and dated.
Actual hours are recorded for at least the first ten pieces of each type and compared with the estimate.
No quote is issued without a margin decision and a minimum-charge check.
documentationEvidence: Cost per productive hour worksheet, dated, with the source of each figure
Quote showing scope, hours basis, exclusions and validity
Job time log with estimated and actual hours
summary: Hours make furniture work visible, so start every quote from stage hours for each piece.
Cost per productive hour uses chargeable time, and includes strippers, finishes and workshop costs.
Gap: no sourced furniture hours exist. Use the Airtasker item ranges only as a sense check, and note that their unit is not stated.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which costs belong in the cost per productive hour for a furniture restorer?
options: Only the hourly wage of the lowest-paid worker
Wages with on-costs, workshop, strippers, finishes, insurance and administration, divided by chargeable hours
The average price of other restorers' items for the year
The deposit and the late fee the client paid

knowledgeChecks.question: A dining chair is estimated at 3 crew-hours and takes 5. What is the right response?
options: Record the actual hours, find the cause, and adjust the estimate and future quotes
Leave the estimate, since the client has already paid
Reduce the crew's paid hours on the next job
Raise the price for this client only and change nothing else

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does a furniture quote need an exclusions list?
options: To hide the margin from the client
To show what the price covers, so hidden damage and scope changes can be priced and disputes are reduced
To lower the client's expectations of the finish

business.gov.au, 'Choose a pricing strategy', https://business.gov.au/products-and-services/choose-a-pricing-strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026. Used for on-costs in the hourly cost.

Airtasker, 'How much does furniture restoration cost?', https://www.airtasker.com/au/costs/furniture-restoration/furniture-restoration-cost, last updated 17 April 2025. Marketplace source; advertised item ranges used as a sense check only. The unit is not stated.
ACCC, 'Setting prices: what's allowed', https://www.accc.gov.au/business/pricing/setting-prices-whats-allowed, last modified 15 July 2026. Used for misleading price statements being prohibited.

NSW Government, LeadSmart, 'Renovating and maintenance', https://www.nsw.gov.au/environment-land-and-water/pollution-contamination/leadsmart-nsw/being-leadsmart/renovating-maintenance, published 18 May 2026, modified 20 July 2026. NSW only.
WorkSafe Victoria, 'Wood dust health hazards and control', https://www.worksafe.vic.gov.au/wood-dust-health-hazards-and-control, reviewed 17 April 2026. Victoria only.
Hypothetical and illustrative figures (22 crew-hours, $60 AUD an hour, 25 per cent margin, 1.5-hour inspection) are invented for this lesson and are not market data.
